Hospital A treats 100 patients: 90 mild cases (85 survive) and 10 severe cases (2 survive) — an overall 87% survival rate. Hospital B treats 100 patients: 10 mild cases (10 survive) and 90 severe cases (60 survive) — an overall 70% survival rate. Within mild cases alone, B survives 100% vs A's 94.4%; within severe cases alone, B survives 66.7% vs A's 20%. Which hospital actually has the higher survival rate within BOTH patient subgroups separately?
choices: This combination of numbers is mathematically impossible
Hospital B, even though Hospital A has the higher overall rate
Hospital A, matching its higher overall rate
They are exactly tied in both subgroups

questions.q: A man leaves his house, turns left three times, and ends up back at his house — where he's confronted by two men wearing masks. Who are these two men?
choices: A baseball catcher and umpire — he's just a player rounding the bases back to home plate
Two burglars breaking into his home
His own reflection in two mirrors

questions.q: You're collecting a set of 6 distinct trading cards. Each pack contains exactly one random card, equally likely to be any of the 6 (duplicates allowed). On average, how many packs do you need to buy to collect all 6 distinct cards at least once?

Alice and Bob each played exactly 5 games of chess today and each won all 5 of their own games, with no draws. Since chess always has exactly one winner per game, how is it possible that both of them won every game they played?
choices: They each played their 5 games against different opponents, not against each other
It's only possible if none of the games were actually finished
One of them must be lying about the results
Chess allows simultaneous draws to count as wins for both sides

questions.q: In Newcomb's paradox, a predictor has already either put $1,000,000 in Box B (if it predicted you'll take only B) or left it empty (if it predicted you'll take both boxes); Box A always visibly holds $1,000. 'Dominance reasoning' says: since the money is already placed, taking both boxes always nets you $1,000 more than taking Box B alone, whatever's inside. 'Expected-utility reasoning', given the predictor's high accuracy, favours taking only Box B. What does this paradox chiefly illustrate?
choices: That the predictor described in the setup is logically impossible
That two-boxing is objectively the mathematically correct choice in all versions
That one-boxing is objectively the mathematically correct choice in all versions
Two seemingly sound decision-theory principles — dominance and expected-utility maximisation — can recommend opposite choices in the very same problem

In a three-way 'truel,' A never misses, B hits 80% of the time, and C hits 50% of the time. They fire in turn (A, then B, then C, repeating), each shooting at the rival they see as the biggest threat, and A moves first with a free choice: shoot at B, shoot at C, or fire into the air on purpose. Which first move gives A the best chance of survival?
choices: Shoot at B, the more dangerous shooter
Shoot at C, the weakest shooter
It makes no difference — A's survival odds are the same regardless
Fire into the air on purpose (deliberately miss)

A fair coin lands heads 5 times in a row. A gambler bets on tails, reasoning 'tails is due.' Is this good reasoning?
choices: No — the streak actually makes heads more likely to continue
Yes, but only because 5 heads in a row is extremely rare
Yes — after 5 heads in a row, tails becomes statistically more likely
No — the coin has no memory; P(tails) is still 0.5 on the next flip regardless of the streak
